title: Holy water at home
hookLine: a font by the door, used when leaving and returning

lines: A CUP BY THE FRONT DOOR.
cards: A small cup screwed to the wall beside a front door, between the light switch and the hook for keys. Sometimes it's a ceramic shell with a saint painted on it. Sometimes it's bone dry; nobody remembered to refill it.
A child heading out to school dips two fingers, touches forehead, chest, one shoulder, the other, and is out the door before the shape is finished.

teach.b: A Catholic walking into a church dips a hand in holy water at the door and makes the sign of the cross. The Church says it recalls baptism, the water a Christian first passed through. Now carry the font home.

teach.h: A FONT BY THE FRONT DOOR.
teach.b: Families can ask a priest to bless water, take it home in a bottle, and fill a small font by the front door.
The church-door gesture now happens at the house door: going out to work, coming back from the hospital, leaving for a first date. Why the door? Thresholds are where a day changes direction.
You walk out into hours you can't control and come back carrying whatever they gave you.

teach.h: KEEP THY COMING IN AND GOING OUT.
teach.b: A psalm has a verse for this, in the Douay-Rheims: "May the Lord keep thy coming in and thy going out; from henceforth now and for ever." The font turns that verse into a gesture.
Before the main Sunday Mass in the older Latin rite, the priest could walk through the church sprinkling the people while the choir sang Asperges me.
The words come from a psalm of repentance, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed: thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow."
Water at the front door says the same thing on a Tuesday morning: wash me, start me again. Like a medal, the water isn't a force field; it doesn't keep accidents off the driveway.
It's a sacramental: a sign, blessed by the Church's prayer, that turns a person toward God at the moment it's easiest to forget, hand on the doorknob, keys in hand, already late.

how: Catholics bless themselves with holy water at the church door, and some families keep a small font of blessed water by the front door at home, making the sign of the cross when leaving and returning.

games.q: what does “holy water at home” mean?
o: water used only by priests at a baptism
blessed water by the door, recalling baptism
a bowl a family uses to wash before meals

games.q: holy water at home — tap the pairs.
p: what the psalm asks God to keep

s: holy water keeps accidents away all by itself
it's a sacramental, a sign that turns a person toward God, not a force field.
the Church says holy water recalls baptism
that's why Catholics bless themselves with it at the church door.
only a priest may use holy water at home
a priest blesses the water; families take it home and use it themselves.

games.q: you're running late, keys in hand, and the font by the door is dry. what is the devotion asking of you?
o: go back and refill it, or you're unprotected today.
a moment of turning toward God at the threshold, water or no water.
skip it; it only counts at church.
games.why: the water is a sign, not a shield. what matters is the turn toward God at the door, and a sign of the cross can carry that alone.

practice: If you have holy water, set it where your hand will find it at the next door you leave by; if not, a sign of the cross at the threshold will do, or a pause with your hand on the handle.
If you pray, borrow the psalm's words, may the Lord keep thy coming in and thy going out; if you don't, let the doorway be one breath before the day takes you.

wordCard.voice: Holy water at home. Blessed water in a small font by the door, used for the sign of the cross going out and coming back: baptism remembered at the threshold.

carryVoice: Your line: going out blessed. Wash me, start me again. Go gently.
